extracted.intended_audience: researchers, publishers, scholarly-communication professionals, and informed members of the public interested in peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles about what makes peer review valuable and how its quality can be recognised, communicated, and improved across publication, funding, and other research workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design anticipates critical scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should anticipate critical scrutiny from the point of designing the research through to reporting it; this leads them to ask critical questions about experimental design, sample size, and reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the study design, sample size, measures and planned analyses were chosen knowing they would face peer scrutiny. Examples/notes: anticipating review encourages better design choices before submission (applies to grant proposals, conference abstracts, and papers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer feedback leads to substantive improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers' comments routinely improve manuscripts and can sometimes utterly transform them; peer review often spots significant methodological flaws in proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether reviewer reports identify methodological weaknesses and whether authors have incorporated corrections that materially improve clarity, rigor, or validity. Example: Sir John Maddox observed that many papers are improved or transformed by reviewers' comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review as an explicit selection/filtering process
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review functions as a selection process that helps funders decide what to fund, editors decide what to publish, and researchers decide what to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging quality, consider how well the review process served its selection purpose — i.e., whether it helped gatekeep for reliability, relevance, and fit for purpose. Note the distinction between evaluating a finished output (publication) and evaluating future work (grant application).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality = ability to answer the research question
rubrics_metrics.description: Define research quality in terms of its ability to answer the question it is addressing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge methods, analysis, and reporting by whether they are appropriate and sufficient to answer the stated research question. Practical checks include adequacy of sample size, experimental controls, and measures of reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make peer review extent and type transparent (peer review statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each paper should include a peer review statement stating what has and hasn’t been reviewed; importantly this statement should also be used in any publicity about the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require and inspect author/publisher statements that specify scope (e.g., main manuscript only, supplementary data not reviewed, light-touch review). Communicate this information in press releases and other public-facing summaries so non-academic audiences understand limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish types and extent of review (classification of review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different types and extents of peer review exist (including 'light touch') and digital/high-volume publishing has increased diversity in standards; users need to know what has been looked at.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a publication, identify whether review was single/double/blind, editorial-only, full peer review, or limited (e.g., scope-limited). Consider establishing simple, standardised labels or questions beyond 'is it peer reviewed?' to capture these differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple, implementable measures and leadership over endless consensus-seeking
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than seeking a global consensus on complex terms, favour some simpler measures and leadership to improve practice now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise feasible, high-impact steps (for example: mandatory review statements, clearer classification of review types) rather than delaying action while debating ideal global metrics. Avoid paralysis by complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate public and media about what peer review means
rubrics_metrics.description: People outside research need to understand the quality checks for research; a simple starter question is 'is it peer reviewed?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use outreach materials (e.g., 'I Don’t Know What to Believe') targeted at journalists, curriculum bodies, parliaments, NGOs and the public to explain what peer review does and does not guarantee. Encourage intermediaries to ask follow-up questions about extent and type of review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train and engage researchers (especially early career) to protect the system
rubrics_metrics.description: Equip the next generation of researchers with the confidence and understanding to participate in and defend peer review as a public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess institutional and community efforts to train early career researchers in reviewing skills, in communicating about peer review, and in understanding both strengths and weaknesses of the system so they will keep concern about quality 'a live consideration.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Align review method to the decision context (publication vs funding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise the important distinction between review for publication (evaluation of a material output) and review for funding (judgement about future work), which differ in objectivity and subjectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing review processes, ensure the review criteria and procedures fit the purpose: selection of finished work (more evidence-based/objective) versus selection of future-oriented proposals (necessarily more interpretive/predictive). Be cautious in communicating equivalence to the public.
